strengths: The author’s proposed system doesn’t require a hand-crafted reward signal to do the second fine-tuning stage.
It is impressive to see how well this works in their experimental results.
The pipeline also seems straightforward to deploy in practice with the understanding that it’s necessary to have large compute available for the foundation models.
The authors also conduct several simulation experiments to validate their system and analyze different components in ablation.
This paper introduces reinforcement learning methods into the training of embodied intelligence models, offering a training approach that is more sample-efficient than supervised learning alone.
The two-stage training method improves training efficiency, and the second phase enables the model to learn a broader range of actions, enhancing its generalizability.
The reinforcement learning section provides detailed explanations of parameter settings.
Experiments with the PaLI model validate the practical effectiveness of this training method, supported by real-world robot testing.
The combination of multimodal foundation agent, supervised fine-tuning, and online self-improvement is a powerful concept that enhances sample efficiency and policy generalization.
The method to generate reward functions using expected value of “steps to go” is novel and effective for RL finetuning.
The proposed approach outperforms supervised learning alone and demonstrates generalization capability to new tasks beyond those observed during training.
This work focuses on a well-defined setting, utilizing a selected foundation model (PaLI-3B) and a policy architecture similar to RT-2.
The methodology is clearly formalized, with key implementation details explicitly provided.
Theoretical insights are also included, offering valuable intuition to aid understanding.
Additionally, the use of figures make an attempt to enhance interpretability.
The author conducts extensive experiments across diverse settings (e.g., LanguageTable, ALOHA, BananaTable) to evaluate the model's capabilities.
Ablation studies on various components (such as the initialization of the foundation model) are performed to demonstrate the necessity and effectiveness of the design choices.
weaknesses: The system requires a second frozen foundation model in the second phase, and storing a second foundation model seems immensely expensive.
Future work should address compressing this second reward foundation model to make the approach more practical.
Real-world robotic experiments need more rigorous evaluation.
The appendix mentions only using a single random seed, which limits evaluation of robustness.
The paper lacks a concluding section, which might impact the overall readability and leave readers without a clear summary of the findings and contributions.
The arguments supporting the model's generalizability are somewhat limited.
The reinforcement learning section would be strengthened by including more theoretical derivations to better explain the underlying principles.

The paper does not sufficiently address the potential limitations of the action discretization method, particularly how the granularity of discretization impacts the model's ability to perform complex or fine-grained manipulations.

The discussion around the choice of the 3B parameter model is weak, lacking a clear justification for why this specific size was chosen over other options, and how this choice might affect the scalability of the method.
The method which combines imitation learning with RL finetuning has been used in various areas of robot learning, limiting the novelty; a paragraph discussing related work is needed.
An ablation study comparing the two-stage approach to pure RL finetuning without the supervised stage should be included.

The novelty of generating reward functions using expected value of “steps to go” is unclear compared to using reference trajectory from dataset/offline policy; a comparison of performance with those methods is needed.
There is a lack of discussion on safety measures or constraints to avoid unreasonable behavior during online RL exploration, especially for fine-grained or contact-rich manipulation tasks.
Many paragraphs are too long, and a lot of content and images are in the appendix, making it difficult to understand the tasks.
All the data are placed in paragraphs; using a table would improve readability.
The use of the time-step variable for the step-to-go loss is constrained to the range [0,T], limiting its generalizability to tasks with arbitrary or longer durations.
The reward function remains static due to reliance on frozen pretrained parameters, possibly hindering further performance improvement.
The experiment in Section 5.1 seems insufficient, as it only explores fine-tuning on a narrow subset of tasks.
Figure 5 is not clearly presented, and its meaning is unclear.

Several experiments modify numerous settings without adequately investigating the effect of these changes through ablation studies; for example, in Section 5.1.3 (ALOHA), settings such as checkpoint selection are altered without analyzing individual component impact.
The related work section could benefit from deeper analysis of how this work differs from prior studies, rather than merely listing them.
The study relies solely on the PaLI-3B model; evaluating the method on additional Vision-Language Foundation Models would provide more comprehensive insights.
